doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Advice on the music business, parents, and Dick Oatts's first night with Thad Jones
summary: Asked about advice, he recalls explaining his New York move to his mother and tells Dick Oatts's story of an instant gig with the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well speaking of the music business I looked at our interview from 1998, and there was this lovely story you told about your parents and your father would call you, like what are you doing today, and you might say, “Well the last couple of days I was at Hamilton College but today I have nothing.” And he would say, “Well you need to get a job.” So my question is what is your advice to students now about the music business. And maybe
it’s pre-Covid. I don’t know if this pandemic should actually affect what you tell students yet. That was a long phrased question, but —

Oh no. It’s a great question. First of all actually what I had to discuss with my father was even better than what you described. He would say, “I know you were at Carnegie Hall last night” and I appreciated it. He and my mother. And I know that you played on a record date and you know, I was so lucky when I lived in New York, I was doing so much. What I would say to kids about that part of your life to and explaining it to your parents is, those challenges are good. It’s good to be able to defend what you’re doing. When I told my mother, I’ll never forget it, we lived on Wood Creek Court I think it was, in Texas. And I said, “Mom, I’m going to move to New York.” And she started crying. She was like, “Why don’t you go back and get your degree?” And this and that. And I had to explain what my vision was for that. And it’s good that I had to do that. You need to be able to tell people what you’re going to do and your strategy. For you to be able to verbalize that not only helps them understand you but it’s for you. You need to outline what path you’re going to take. Sometimes you don’t know that path and you’re on faith and you can say that too. Say I don’t know what it is but in my gut I know I need to be around the musicians that I’ve adored all my life. And sometimes that’s enough but if you can add to it you can. I’ll give you a quick story of somebody else. Do you know Dick Oatts, the great sax player? He’s a great alto player. Yeah. So Dick said he worked with Thad Jones at University of Minnesota. That’s where I first met Thad Jones, I lived in Minnesota. And Thad loved him. He said, “Man you sound great.” He says, “Look if you ever move to New York give me a call.” He was like wow, cool. So he flew into LaGuardia Airport about a year later and there was a pay phone there at LaGuardia Airport and he goes, “Hey Thad, I’m here.” But now here’s where it gets crazy. Thad goes, “Oh man, I remember you, Minnesota, alto player.” He said, “What are you doing tonight?” And Dick said, “Nothing.” He says, “We need a second alto” or something. This is like when he lands in LaGuardia from Minnesota. You know? So he went and I said, “How was that first night?” Here’s the funny part of the story. He goes, well — I don’t know if you ever saw the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band but it was an amazing band that was totally spontaneous. It was also like a party many times, what they did on the bandstand. It was good times and just fun. And you never knew what Thad was going to do. I remember myself seeing that band a lot. He’d just cut off the whole band and Janice Robinson would just play trombone with her plunger, and then Thad would join her and they would talk with their plungers you know. And it was like you knew that they were swearing and arguing and telling jokes with their instruments. So anyway Dick was like I wonder if he’s going to give me a solo.
